..

Rest of Today through Monday...

Upper level pattern is pretty benign for today with zonal westerly
flow aloft and only weak energy crossing the area. Underneath that
though there is persistent southeasterly flow working into SE
Montana that will boost afternoon CAPE values to around 2000j/kg
and producing enough shear to support a chance for a few strong to
severe thunderstorms. Previous model runs kept convective
initiation just to the east of the forecast area, but the 12z runs
are further east developing convection from Fallon south into
Carter county between 1pm and 5pm. Strong winds (60-70mph) and 
heavy rain will be the main threats with any storms that do 
develop over this area today, with large hail being a secondary 
threat. The limiting factor will be energy available to kick start
the convection as the energy aloft looks weak and mainly 
streamwise which is less conducive to lifting the atmosphere. The 
HRRR seems to be downplaying the western initiation and the upper 
dynamics, generating initial convection over the eastern Black 
Hills, which actually seems pretty reasonable. However can't 
ignore the other models, especially with a large outdoor event in 
Alzada this afternoon. Wouldn't be surprised to see the SPC 18z 
outlook push the marginal/slight risk further west to cover the 
latest model guidance. 

The rest of the area will be war and dry with the aforementioned
westerly flow over the area suppressing convection. Smoke
concentrations look to increase this afternoon over the western
half of the forecast area as the HRRR is advecting in significant
smoke from the fires in SW Montana today. Highs this afternoon
will be mainly in the low to mid 90s. Overnight lows will be in
the 60s for much of the area thanks to the smoke holding in the
heat. Western valley locations will drop into the mid 50s. 

Set up for Wednesday looks similar to today, with the exception of
a stronger upper disturbance arriving early afternoon from the
southwest, crossing areas from Big Horn/Sheridan County northeast
through Fallon County. This will bring a more widespread threat
for convection, however the shear and CAPE will both be weaker, so
less of a threat for strong to severe storms. Best chance for a
stronger storm or two will remain over the SE Montana. PWAT values
increase Wednesday with higher values pushing further west.
Combined with weaker shear/storm motion the potential for locally
heavy rainfall with any storms is enhances. WPC has issued a
marginal risk for excessive rainfall (Flash Flood potential) for
the eastern 3/4 of the forecast area Wednesday to cover this
increase in available moisture. 

Persistent east-southeast low level winds will continue to
advect low level moisture into the area Thursday/Friday while
monsoonal moisture increases aloft. This will produce a very juicy
atmosphere over the area for this time of year. Southwest flow
will be over the area during this period with occasional
disturbances crossing us, providing lift for more widespread
shower and thunderstorm activity. It won't take much to kick off
precipitation given the amount of water in the atmosphere (3 to 4
standard deviations above normal) during this period. GEFS
precipitation percentiles are showing forecast precipitation
amounts in the 95th to 99th percentile for the eastern 2/3 of the
forecast area Thursday into Friday, so climatically this is a high
end precipitation event being forecast by the models. WPC 
probabilities for half an inch or more precipitation shows 
widespread 50-100% chances across the forecast area Thu- Fri, with
probabilities for 1+ inches above 50% from Rosebud County east 
into the Dakotas. WPC has a slight risk for excessive rainfall 
(flash flood potential) from a Roundup to Billings line eastward 
for Thursday into Friday morning. With the precipitation and cloud
cover, along with a general north/northeast wind, will see 
temperatures drop well below normal for Thu/Fri, with highs 
expected in the 70s both days.

Saturday has the potential to remain unsettled and cool, but some
models are starting a warming and drying trend Saturday. For now
the NBM is leaning cool and unsettled and the official forecast
reflects that, but wouldn't be surprised to see this period trend
warmer and drier as southerly winds take hold. 

Sunday into Monday shows a ridge bulging northward along the spine
of the Rockies into our vicinity, thanks to a persistent and at
times digging upper trof just off the west coast. This should 
bring temperatures back toward seasonal levels and decrease 
precipitation chances. That said, depending on how much rain falls
Thu-Sat, there may be plenty of residual moisture to support at 
least decent afternoon and evening precipitation chances each day.
Chambers
